column5: Commentary's 12:36 prison dream; grapes pressed into a cup
column6: The imprisoned cupbearer dreams of taking grapes and pressing them into Pharaoh's cup, giving the commentary's prison grape-press scene in its own narrative setting.

column5: Wine with no vent; new wineskins ready to burst
column6: The commentary's cork holds squeezed liquid in a bottle; Elihu instead likens unspoken words to fermenting wine with no vent, so the same containment intensifies pressure toward rupture.

column5: Locked garden; sealed spring
column6: The commentary's stopper keeps the bitter extract inside its vessel; the poem's sealed spring likewise contains a source, but presents closure as erotic exclusivity rather than medicine.

column5: Living fountain; cracked cisterns
column6: The commentary ends with a sealed bottle that retains its medicinal essence, whereas Jeremiah's chosen cisterns are cracked and cannot hold water, making failed containment a charge against Judah.

column5: Marah's bitter water and the wood
column6: At Marah the people cannot drink bitter water until Moses throws a tree into it and it becomes sweet; this reverses the commentary's bitter tree extract, which remains bitter yet is named medicine.

column5: YHWH as healer
column6: After the bitter-water episode, YHWH identifies himself as Israel's healer; this makes explicit the healing frame that the commentary gives to bitter sabr, though the remedy and bitterness work differently.

column5: Judah trodden as grapes in a winepress
column6: The lament says the Lord has trodden Judah like grapes in a press; the commentary's human squeezed into loss becomes a crushed people here, and the press yields devastation rather than a useful essence.

column5: Winepress trodden in wrath; blood on garments
column6: The divine speaker treads the press in anger and blood stains his clothing, a direct counter-image to the commentary's extracted juice as good and generous giving.

column5: Ripe harvest; vats overflowing with wickedness
column6: The harvest press overflows because the nations' wickedness is great; the shared pressing and yield imagery makes the commentary's beneficial extract read against a judgment harvest.

column5: Fig cake applied to a boil; recovery
column6: Isaiah orders a fig cake laid on Hezekiah's boil and Hezekiah recovers; this gives a concrete plant-based remedy alongside the commentary's bitter tree extract called medicine.

column5: Medicines created from the earth
column6: Sirach says the Lord made medicines from the earth and a sensible person does not reject them; it supplies a Jewish wisdom frame for the commentary's medicinal plant exudate as a beneficial natural substance.

column5: Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
column6: The Hebrew verb עצר closes the heavens so rain and yield cease; this restraint is the agricultural inverse of the commentary's squeezing that releases juice and, in its Yusuf comparison, marks relief after scarcity.

column5: Commentary label root خ س ر; Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
column6: Moses says Israel lacked nothing during the wilderness years; the cognate sense of lack gives a direct counter-reading to the commentary's human placed in decrease and loss.

column5: Commentary label root ء ن س; Hebrew אנש, regular sound correspondence and BDB Arabic-cognate note
column6: Job asks what אנוש, a mortal human, is that God gives him such attention; it lends the commentary's generic human between pressure and loss a specific mortal and vulnerable register.

column5: Treasure in earthen vessels
column6: Paul places treasure in fragile earthen vessels; this gives a close vessel image for the commentary's bottled essence, while locating the value in the vessel's contents rather than in a bitter remedy.

column5: Afflicted but not crushed
column6: Paul says the community is pressed yet not crushed; this directly answers the commentary's image of the human as squeezed matter that decreases, with pressure failing to exhaust the people.

column5: Struck down but not destroyed
column6: Paul distinguishes being struck down from being destroyed; this counters the commentary's equation of human pressure with decrease by describing survival after blows.

column5: Tribulation produces endurance
column6: Paul says affliction produces endurance, which gives the commentary's squeezed, bitter sabr a developmental reading: pressure can generate the quality that sustains a person.

column5: God's love poured into hearts
column6: Paul says God's love has been poured into believers' hearts; the commentary specifically notes Qur'anic patience poured over people, and this supplies a Christian liquid metaphor for an inward virtue, while naming love rather than patience.

column5: Painful discipline later yields peaceful fruit
column6: Discipline is painful in the present but later yields peaceful fruit; this gives a precise interpretive bridge to the commentary's bitter medicine, whose discomfort is paired with healing benefit.

column5: Saints' endurance, God's commands, and faith in Jesus
column6: The verse defines the saints by endurance, keeping God's commands, and faith in Jesus; this closely gathers patience, faithful action, and belief in the kind of people the commentary exempts from loss.

column5: Persistence in doing good and harvest in due season
column6: Paul urges doing good without weariness because a harvest comes in due time if one does not give up; this joins the commentary's righteous action and patience to an agricultural yield.

column5: Stirring one another to love and good works
column6: The addressees are told to provoke one another toward love and good works; this closely matches the commentary's reciprocal counsel and righteous deeds, though it specifies love rather than truth.

column5: Encouraging one another
column6: The assembly is to encourage one another as the day approaches; this supplies the reciprocal communal action behind the commentary's repeated mutual exhortation.

column5: Turning a wanderer back from truth
column6: James addresses fellow believers and says that whoever turns a brother back from wandering from the truth performs a communal corrective act like the commentary's mutual counsel in truth.

column5: Saving a soul from death
column6: James adds that bringing the wanderer back saves that person's soul from death; this makes the truth-directed mutual correction a rescue from loss, not merely instruction.

column5: Speak truth each with the neighbor
column6: Paul commands each person to put away falsehood and speak truth with the neighbor because they belong to one another; this is a direct communal truth-speaking analogue to the commentary's mutual counsel.

column5: Perseverance in doing good leads to eternal life
column6: Paul describes those who persist in doing good and seek glory and immortality as receiving eternal life; this combines the commentary's good action and patience in a salvific outcome.

column5: Salvation as a gift through faith
column6: Paul says salvation is by grace through faith and is God's gift; set beside the commentary's list of belief and righteous deeds, this frames the ground of rescue differently.

column5: Not from works, so no one may boast
column6: Paul explicitly denies that salvation is from works, while the commentary includes righteous deeds in the description of those outside loss; the contrast concerns how deeds relate to rescue.

column5: Created for good works
column6: Paul immediately says believers are created in Christ for good works; this keeps the contrast from erasing action and offers a distinct account of deeds as the intended result of salvation.

column5: Faith and patience inherit the promises
column6: The author urges imitation of those who inherit promises through faith and patience; this directly pairs two qualities named in the commentary's saved group.

column5: Steadfast work is not in vain
column6: Paul calls the community steadfast and abundant in the Lord's work, assuring them that their labor is not empty; this counters the commentary's language of human loss with enduring good action.

column5: Testing of faith produces endurance
column6: James says the testing of faith produces endurance; this gives the commentary's bitter, pressed sabr an explicit formation process under trial.

column5: Endurance completes its work
column6: James says endurance must have its full effect so people become complete; this interprets patience as a formed quality with a beneficial end, like the commentary's medicine metaphor.

column5: Daily mutual exhortation prevents hardening
column6: The community must exhort one another daily so no one is hardened by sin's deceit; this gives the commentary's mutual counsel a concrete protective purpose against moral loss.

column5: Enduring suffering while doing good
column6: Peter asks what credit there is in enduring punishment for wrongdoing, then calls it grace to endure suffering while doing good; this tightly joins patient endurance to righteous action.

column5: The farmer patiently waits for precious fruit
column6: James tells the community to wait patiently like a farmer for the earth's precious crop; it links patience to delayed yield, though the image is cultivation rather than extraction.

column5: Eucharist as medicine of immortality
column6: Ignatius calls the shared Eucharist medicine of immortality and an antidote to death; this Christian interpretation turns the commentary's medicinal image toward communal nourishment and rescue from death.

column5: Honoring God with wealth
column6: The verse commands honoring YHWH with one's wealth and first produce; beside the commentary's claim that extracted juice figures good and generosity, it makes abundance an act of giving.

column5: Vats filled with new wine
column6: The next verse promises vats brimming with new wine; the commentary's juice as beneficial abundance finds a concrete biblical image of overflowing produce.

column5: Wine gladdens the human heart
column6: The psalm names wine as what gladdens the human heart; it gives a biblical instance of the commentary's extracted juice as goodness for people.

column5: Wine gladdens God and humans
column6: In Jotham's fable the vine says its wine gladdens God and people; this concretely parallels the commentary's report that Arabs make expressed juice a figure for good and generosity.

column5: A winepress prepared for grapes but wild grapes produced
column6: The vineyard owner builds a winepress expecting good grapes but finds wild grapes; the image makes the commentary's generous essence contingent on a yield that can instead disappoint.

column5: Seven years of famine after seven years of plenty
column6: Joseph's dream interpretation predicts seven lean years after abundance; it parallels the commentary's sequence of scarcity and eventual relief while preserving a different order from its pressing year.

column5: Storehouses opened during famine
column6: When famine covers the land, Joseph opens the storehouses; this connects the commentary's retained essence in a closed bottle with stored provision later released to sustain people.

column5: Wine left on its lees and not poured between vessels
column6: Moab's undisturbed wine retains its flavor because it has not been poured from vessel to vessel; the commentary's cork likewise preserves a liquid, but Jeremiah makes stillness a figure for complacency.

column5: The cup of divine wrath and its dregs
column6: The psalm's cup contains foaming wine and dregs that the wicked must drink; it turns contained liquid toward judgment rather than the commentary's medicinal extract.

column5: Maror eaten to recall Egyptian oppression
column6: At the Passover meal bitter herbs are part of the narrated memory of bondage; this makes bitterness a communal ritual of remembered suffering, unlike the commentary's bitter remedy.

column5: Fish gall and restored sight
column6: Tobit's father regains sight after fish gall is applied; this is a concrete natural-substance cure alongside the commentary's medicinal tree exudate, though its source is animal rather than plant.

column5: Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
column6: The Hebrew form עצר says YHWH had closed every womb in Abimelech's house; this related closure gives a bodily analogue to the commentary's stopper sealing a vessel, with withheld fertility instead of preserved medicine.

column5: Commentary label root خ س ر; Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
column6: Abraham asks whether five righteous people might be lacking from fifty; the Hebrew cognate makes decrease numerical and ties the missing count to whether a city is spared.

column5: Colleagues sharpen one another in Torah
column6: The Talmud applies iron sharpening iron to scholars who sharpen one another in Torah; this interprets mutual counsel as reciprocal learning and correction, a specific Jewish account of the commentary's tawāṣī relation.

column5: Iron sharpens iron
column6: The proverb says one person sharpens another as iron sharpens iron; this gives mutual exhortation a concrete image of improvement through another's words.

column5: Accept what comes and be patient in humiliation
column6: Sirach tells the reader to accept what comes and be patient in humiliation; it links patience to receiving painful experience, an explicit bridge to the commentary's bitter remedy.

column5: Gold tested in fire; acceptable people in humiliation
column6: Sirach compares tested people to gold in a furnace; it supplies a refining image in which affliction tests and qualifies, alongside the commentary's pressure that produces bitter sabr.

column5: Correct, rebuke, and exhort with patience and teaching
column6: Paul charges Timothy to preach, correct, and exhort with patience and teaching; unlike the commentary's mutual practice, this is a ministerial instruction, but it joins truth-directed correction to patience.

column5: Endurance produces tested character and hope
column6: Paul says endurance produces tested character and hope; this continues the commentary's image of a beneficial quality formed through pressure.

column5: Commentary label root ص ب ر; Hebrew צבר, table sound correspondence only
column6: The Hebrew verb צבר describes Joseph piling up grain beyond measure; beside the commentary's corked bottle retaining squeezed essence, the narrow connection is accumulation and storage, not a shared sense of patience.

column5: Commentary label root ء ن س; Aramaic אנש, table sound correspondence only and unverified
column6: Daniel sees one like a bar enash, a humanlike figure who receives dominion; this contrasts the commentary's collective humanity with a singular exalted use of the related Aramaic word.

column5: Tongue of the infant clings from thirst
column6: The commentary names a thirst-dried tongue as maʿṣūr; in Jerusalem's siege the infant's tongue clings to the palate for thirst, making the bodily image concrete in a scene of deprivation.

column5: Tongue fails for thirst; water is promised
column6: The needy have no water and their tongue fails from thirst; this closely matches the commentary's dried tongue, while Isaiah's promised springs reverse depletion with relief.

column5: Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
column6: The proverb names the closed womb with עצר; this table correspondence links the commentary's root to bodily closure, while the proverb's unsatisfied earth and water add a distinct thirst setting.

column5: Closed womb and earth unsatisfied with water
column6: The proverb places a closed womb beside earth that is never satisfied with water; this meets the commentary's closure and thirst images together, but as unsated lack rather than a bottle retaining medicine.

column5: Bitter water that brings a curse
column6: The suspected woman is made to drink water of bitterness that brings a curse; this is a concrete counter-use of bitter liquid beside the commentary's bitter plant extract called medicine.

column5: Bitter water brings bodily affliction
column6: The ritual's consequence is that the water becomes bitter within the woman and brings a curse; bitterness here exposes and punishes rather than healing as in the commentary's medicinal sabr.

column5: Bitterness and wormwood as affliction
column6: The speaker says he has been filled with bitterness and wormwood; the plant bitterness is imposed misery, a counter-reading to the commentary's painful but beneficial remedy.

column5: Wormwood makes waters bitter and kills many
column6: The star named Wormwood makes the waters bitter and many die from them; this directly reverses the commentary's bitter plant extract as medicine by making bitter liquid lethal.

column5: Scroll sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach
column6: John is told to eat the scroll, which will be sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach; the two-stage taste gives the commentary's swallowed bitter medicine a distinct prophetic counterpart.

column5: Sweet taste turns bitter after eating
column6: John reports that the scroll tasted sweet and then made his stomach bitter; this locates bitterness after ingestion, unlike the commentary's bitter extract whose bitterness is already the medicinal quality.

column5: Wine mixed with gall is offered and refused
column6: Jesus is offered wine mixed with gall and refuses it after tasting; this gives a specific bitter drink in a suffering scene, but the text presents no healing benefit like the commentary's medicine.

column5: Wine mixed with myrrh is refused
column6: Mark says wine mixed with myrrh is offered to Jesus and he does not take it; the plant resin in a wine drink recalls the commentary's plant-derived bitter essence, though Mark does not call it bitter or medicinal.

column5: Jesus says he thirsts
column6: At the crucifixion Jesus says he thirsts; this is a specific bodily thirst scene beside the commentary's dried tongue, with the speaker's impending death making the need unresolved.

column5: Sour wine lifted to the thirsty Jesus
column6: The bystanders raise sour wine to Jesus after he says he thirsts; the drink is acidic relief in a death scene, not the beneficial bitter remedy described in the commentary.

column5: New wine bursts wineskins
column6: Jesus says new wine put into old wineskins bursts them and both wine and skins are lost; unlike the commentary's corked bottle retaining a medicinal essence, this vessel fails under pressure and causes loss.

column5: Earth's grapes thrown into the winepress of wrath
column6: The angel gathers the earth's grapes and throws them into God's great winepress; this directly turns the commentary's pressing that yields good essence into an apocalyptic harvest of wrath.

column5: Winepress trodden; blood flows out
column6: The press is trodden outside the city and blood flows from it; this specifies the destructive yield of the preceding winepress, in contrast to the commentary's useful extracted juice.

column5: Jar of meal and jug of oil do not fail during drought
column6: Elijah promises that the widow's jar and jug will not be emptied until rain returns; the contained provision in scarcity parallels the commentary's stored essence and its Yusuf scene of relief after famine.

column5: The jar and jug remain supplied
column6: The narrative says the widow's jar and jug did not fail as promised; this continuation shows stored liquid and food sustaining life through drought, unlike a one-time extracted dose.

column5: Oil fills every borrowed vessel and then stops
column6: The widow's oil keeps filling containers until there is no vessel left, when the flow stops; it gives a precise parallel to liquid collected and held by a vessel, with provision released rather than a corked medicine.

column5: Treader of grapes overtaken by the sower; hills drip wine
column6: Amos pictures restoration so abundant that grape-treading overlaps sowing and mountains drip sweet wine; this makes pressing the sign of relief and plenty, as in the commentary's post-scarcity year.

column5: Gideon threshes wheat in a winepress to hide it
column6: Gideon works grain in a winepress while hiding from Midianite raiders; the press belongs to threatened subsistence here, unlike the commentary's press as the sign that scarcity has ended.

column5: Commentary label root خ س ر; Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
column6: The verse says young lions lack and hunger while those who seek YHWH lack no good thing; Hebrew חסר gives the commentary's decrease a direct cognate contrast between want and provision.

column5: Put on patience with other virtues
column6: Paul tells the community to put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience; this places patience among shared ethical dispositions, extending the commentary's community defined by sabr.

column5: Bear with and forgive one another
column6: The addressees are told to bear with and forgive one another; this gives the commentary's mutual counsel in patience a concrete practice of forbearance.

column5: Teach and admonish one another with the word
column6: Paul tells the community to teach and admonish one another with wisdom as Christ's word dwells among them; this is a close communal counterpart to mutual counsel in truth.

column5: Admonish, encourage, help, and be patient with all
column6: Paul urges the church to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone; this combines mutual moral care with patience in concrete cases.

column5: Seek the good of one another and everyone
column6: The church must not repay evil for evil but always pursue good for one another and all; this connects reciprocal ethical counsel to doing good.

column5: The Lord's servant must be patient and able to teach
column6: Paul describes the Lord's servant as not quarrelsome but patient and able to teach; this joins patient conduct to truthful instruction, though it is pastoral rather than reciprocal.

column5: Correct opponents gently toward knowledge of truth
column6: The servant is to correct opponents gently in hope that God grants them knowledge of truth; this directly joins correction and truth, adding a one-directional teaching scene to the commentary's mutual counsel.

column5: Can faith without works save?
column6: James asks whether a person who claims faith but has no works can be saved; this directly tests the commentary's pairing of belief and righteous action, making their relation explicit.

column5: Faith without works is dead
column6: James says faith without works is dead; this gives a specific Christian account of why belief and deeds belong together in the commentary's exception from loss.

column5: Disobedience to truth brings wrath
column6: Paul contrasts those who obey truth with those who disobey truth and pursue unrighteousness, who receive wrath; this counters the commentary's mutual truth-counsel by depicting refusal of truth as a path to judgment.

column5: Losing life for Jesus saves it
column6: Jesus says the one who loses life for his sake will save it; this reverses the commentary's general human loss into a paradoxical self-loss that leads to rescue.

column5: Enduring trial leads to the crown of life
column6: James calls blessed the person who endures trial and promises the crown of life; this connects patience under pressure to a salvific outcome.

column5: Tested faith compared with refined gold
column6: Peter says tested faith, more precious than perishable gold refined by fire, will result in praise and honor; this gives pressure a refining yield, though by fire rather than squeezing.

column5: Pruning a fruitful branch for more fruit
column6: Jesus says the vinedresser prunes the fruitful branch so it bears more fruit; this gives the commentary's grape and pressure images a contrasting cultivation model where cutting increases future yield.

column5: Jesus asks that the cup pass, then submits
column6: Jesus asks whether the cup can pass but submits to the Father's will; the cup makes suffering a drink-like burden, while the scene adds willing endurance rather than the commentary's extracted medicine.

column5: Jesus accepts the cup he must drink
column6: Jesus says that if the cup cannot pass unless he drinks it, the Father's will be done; this continuation turns the cup from a requested escape into accepted suffering.

column5: God supplies seed and increases the harvest of righteousness
column6: Paul uses seed, bread, and an increased harvest of righteousness; this connects agricultural yield to the commentary's good essence and gives generosity an ethical harvest image.

column5: Enrichment for generosity
column6: Paul says the community is enriched in every way for generosity; this closely matches the commentary's report that expressed juice serves as a figure for goodness and giving.

column5: Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
column6: The proverb's closed womb uses the Hebrew root the table matches to Arabic ع ص ر; it supplies a bodily use of closure distinct from pressing and from the bottle-stopper sense in the commentary.
